tiers.criteria: Clean separation of concerns with clear module boundaries. Appropriate design patterns applied (not forced). Layer dependencies are unidirectional. Service boundaries align with business domains. Considers horizontal scalability. No circular dependencies. Consistent with existing system architecture style.
Good separation of concerns. Mostly appropriate patterns. Minor architectural smells. Compatible with existing architecture.
Reasonable structure but some design issues: 2-3 unclear module boundaries, or a pattern choice that doesn't fit well. Would require some rework for production.
Significant structural issues: tight coupling between modules, inappropriate patterns, or design that ignores the existing system architecture.
Fundamentally flawed: monolithic design for a microservice context, or fragmented into too many services with excessive inter-service calls.

RESTful conventions followed consistently. All endpoints have clear request/response schemas with types. Proper HTTP methods and status codes. Pagination for list endpoints. Idempotency for mutations. Versioning strategy stated. Error response format standardized. Authentication/authorization specified per endpoint.
Good API design with minor gaps: missing pagination on a list endpoint, or inconsistent error format. Most endpoints well-defined.
APIs defined but with notable issues: missing response schemas, inconsistent naming conventions, or missing error handling specification.
Minimal API definition. Only endpoint paths listed without detailed schemas. Major design issues.
No meaningful API design, or APIs that contradict RESTful principles throughout.

All entities identified with complete field definitions (name, type, constraints). Relationships properly modeled (FK, junction tables for M:N). Appropriate indexes for query patterns. Soft delete where appropriate. Audit fields (created_at, updated_at). Enum types for status fields.
Good schema covering all main entities. Relationships correct. Minor gaps: missing an index, or incomplete field constraints.
Main entities present but some incomplete: missing fields, or relationships not properly modeled.
Incomplete schema: missing 1-2 important entities, or fundamental relationship errors.
Minimal or incorrect schema that would not support the required functionality.

All integration points with existing services clearly identified with interface contracts. Respects existing auth patterns. Uses existing infrastructure appropriately. Backward compatibility considered. Failure handling at integration points specified.
Integration points identified. Uses existing infrastructure. Minor gaps in failure handling or boundary specification.
Acknowledges existing services but integration details are vague. Some unverified assumptions.
Ignores some existing system constraints. Proposes redundant infrastructure.
Designs in isolation, ignoring the existing system context entirely.
Key technical decisions have explicit justification with alternatives considered. Performance implications discussed. At least 2 technical risks identified with mitigation strategies.
Some decisions justified with alternatives mentioned. 1-2 risks identified. Trade-off thinking is present but not thorough.
Decisions made without justification. One risk mentioned in passing. Little evidence of alternative evaluation.
No trade-off analysis. Design presented as the only option. No risk awareness.
Design choices contradict the stated constraints without acknowledgment.

hard_caps.condition: Design introduces circular dependencies or creates a distributed monolith
Design provides no API contracts (just endpoint names without request/response schemas)
Design has no database schema or only lists table names without fields/types/relationships
Design completely ignores the existing system context
Systemic vs isolated: missing index on one table in otherwise thoughtful schema is 16/20, not 8/20

calibration_persona: You are a principal engineer reviewing a technical design for a high-traffic production system. Grade based on whether this design could actually be built, deployed, and maintained — not on whether it reads well as a document. Avoid leniency bias (being impressed by comprehensive diagrams while missing fundamental architectural flaws) AND paranoia (penalizing reasonable simplifications in a first-iteration design).
